title: The farewell admonition
hook: an admonition that made eyes weep: hold to my sunnah and the rightly guided after me (Nawawi 28, al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah)
tomorrow: Mu'adh asks what leads to the Garden. why does it end at his tongue?

segments.voice: Yesterday: ask your heart. Before that: the basics, done well. Purity is half. No oppression. Every glory is a gift. Every joint, every day. Today, the one about holding on.
screen: `THE BASICS, DONE WELL · PURITY IS HALF · NO OPPRESSION` → `EVERY GLORY IS A GIFT · EVERY JOINT, EVERY DAY · ASK YOUR HEART`

segments.voice: A talk so moving the listeners cried: what did they ask for next? Graduation speeches, last days at a job, goodbyes at an airport gate. The jokes fade; the one line near the end tends to stay. Last words are the ones people tend to keep. Al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once gave them an admonition that made hearts tremble and eyes weep. Someone said: this sounds like a farewell. So advise us.
screen: `LAST WORDS GET KEPT.` → `HEARTS TREMBLED. EYES WEPT.` → `SO ADVISE US.`

segments.voice: That's al-Nawawi's twenty-eighth hadith, from Sunan Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase. He counseled them to be mindful of Allah, and to listen and obey, even if the one put in charge is a slave. Whoever lives on among you will see a great deal of disagreement. So hold to my sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me; bite onto it with your molars. And beware of newly invented matters. Molars. Not the front teeth, the ones that nibble. The back ones, the ones that grip and don't let go, even while the rest of the mouth is busy talking. It's a picture of holding on while something pulls the other way. When everyone's arguing, keep your grip. A grip isn't a fist swinging at everyone else. It's teeth closed on what you were given, while the noise goes past. It echoes an earlier day of this block, too: keep it as it came. Beware of newly invented matters is the same worry, that what's handed down gets quietly rewritten. And it's a good place to stand at the end of two weeks. The basics. The water. The tip jar. The beads. The joints. The heart. Not a list to master all at once. One or two things to bite down on.
screen: `HEARTS TREMBLED. SO ADVISE US.` · `MUCH DISAGREEMENT AHEAD.` · `HOLD TO THE SUNNAH.` · `BITE ON IT WITH YOUR MOLARS.` · then, large: `HOLD IT WITH YOUR MOLARS.`

segments.voice: Write by hand one practice you want to keep a grip on: a sunnah of the Prophet's, like a greeting or a smile, or one thing from these two weeks. One line, no explaining. Then hold the paper for the sit, grip light but steady, the way you'd hold something you plan to keep.
The farewell admonition: the talk that made eyes weep, and its charge: hold to the sunnah, and hold it with your molars.
To keep: hold it with your molars, the back teeth, the ones that don't let go. Two weeks of the forty, carried.

screen: `DAY 1456 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY · 28 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: MU'ADH ASKS WHAT LEADS TO THE GARDEN. WHY DOES IT END AT HIS TONGUE?`

howItsDone: Muslims cite this hadith on keeping to the sunnah through disagreement; Sunni teachers name the rightly guided caliphs as Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, and the 'molars' image is often quoted on its own.

chat.meaning: The farewell charge: hold to the sunnah with your molars. A real grip on one thing, not a loose hand on everything.

al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah.meaning: the companion who reported the farewell admonition

sunnah.meaning: the Prophet's way: what he said, did and approved

caliphs.meaning: the Prophet's successors who led the community after him

Sunan Abu Dawud.meaning: a hadith collection compiled by Abu Dawud

al-Nawawi.meaning: the scholar from Syria who gathered the Forty

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): review shape. Review: the six carries of days 1450–1455 return in the review voice and games.recall; today's word is taught lightly. 'Even if the one put in charge is a slave' is in the hadith; kept plain without comment; confirm the paraphrase reads fairly for a modern audience.

howItsDone names the four rightly guided caliphs as Sunni usage; Shia Muslims read 'the rightly guided after me' differently (e.g. as the Imams of the Prophet's family). Consider adding a line if the Keeper wants both views stated.
This hadith (al-'Irbad's 'farewell-like admonition') is distinct from the Farewell Sermon at the Hajj; the guess game uses that confusion as a wrong option.
